messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: restricted order of lower=, upper=
parts:
In order to get Stan to compile on Windows,
I reduced the grammar complexity so that only
the following are legal:

int<lower=L,upper=U>
int<lower=L>
int<upper=U>

Two cases from the fully general definition are
missing:

int<upper=U,lower=L>
int<>

Ditto for "real".

Although it doesn't seem like much, it cut down
on the complexity of the grammar rules.

The question is whether we want to allow the
backwards order. I see some benefit in eliminating
the two cases that are missing.

Also, should I do the same thing for truncation,
as in converting

y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,];

to

y ~ normal(0,1) T<lower=1>;

I prefer the interval notation, because the angle
brackets evoke type constraints for me due to
C++ and Java.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: restricted order of lower=, upper=
parts:
The transform uses the scaled inverse logit.

x = low + (high - low) * inv_logit(y)

If low == high, then x = low.

The gradient is zero in this case, but the
random momentum will keep y flying around, which
should be OK.

I need to make sure to add some error checking.
There isn't any right now! And then I need to
doc the behavior clearly.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: restricted order of lower=, upper=
parts:
This might be ok sometimes, but it probably won't be in general.
Consider the scenario where the initial momentum for y is large
compared to the momenta for the other variables. y is going to get a
good running start in some random direction, and the other variables'
trajectories are going to take a little while to turn around. But by
the time they do, the overall trajectory will be dominated by the y
dimension, so we'll never satisfy the u-turn criterion, so each
iteration runs until we reach max_treedepth.

Basically, improper posteriors are always trouble.

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: added !(lower < upper) constraint to transform
parts:
I changed lub_constrain in prob/transform so that
it throws a std domain error if !(lower < upper).

I also changed the lub_constrain w/o Jacobians so
that it is bounded away from 0 and 1 like the one
with Jacobians. (See the previous message for more
on the ramifications for gradients.)

More on Matt's point about NUTS below.
